conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: What is advance care planning, and why does it matter?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: The process by which a person with capacity records their wishes for future care/treatment, so that if they later lose capacity their voice still guides decisions. It sits at the meeting of medical law and end-of-life practice.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: Which statute underpins advance care planning and adult consent in England & Wales?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: The Mental Capacity Act 2005. An advance document only becomes relevant once capacity for that specific decision is lost.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: List the 5 statutory principles of the Mental Capacity Act 2005.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: (1) Presume capacity unless established otherwise. (2) Support the person to decide (all practicable help) before deeming them unable. (3) An unwise decision does not equal lack of capacity. (4) Act in the person's best interests if they lack capacity. (5) Choose the least restrictive option.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: Describe the 2-stage capacity test.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: Stage 1: is there an impairment of, or disturbance in, the mind/brain? Stage 2: does it mean the person cannot understand, retain, use/weigh, or communicate the decision? Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: Does an unwise decision indicate a lack of capacity?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: No. A capacitous adult can refuse any treatment (even life-saving) for any or no reason — an unwise choice is not incapacity (e.g. a Jehovah's Witness refusing blood).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: What is the hierarchy of end-of-life documents by legal force?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: 1. Advance Decision to Refuse Treatment (ADRT) — legally binding. 2. Lasting Power of Attorney (LPA) — appoints a decision-maker. 3. Advance statement — influential but NOT binding.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: What is an Advance Decision to Refuse Treatment (ADRT)?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: A 'living will' — lets an adult refuse specified treatments in advance, to apply if they later lose capacity. A valid and applicable ADRT is legally binding — the same force as a contemporaneous refusal by a competent patient; overriding it risks battery/liability.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: What can an ADRT NOT do?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: It can only refuse treatment — never demand/request a specific treatment, and never anything unlawful (euthanasia/assisted dying are illegal in the UK). It cannot refuse basic care (warmth, hygiene, oral food/fluids) or symptom relief.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: What makes an ADRT valid and applicable?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: The person was ≥18 and had capacity when making it; it specifies the treatment refused + circumstances; it has not been withdrawn or contradicted by later behaviour; and the current circumstances are not materially different from those anticipated.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: What extra formalities are required for an ADRT to refuse LIFE-SUSTAINING treatment?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: It must be in writing, signed, and witnessed, and explicitly state it applies 'even if life is at risk' (the single most-tested detail). If these aren't met it is not binding, but still counts as evidence of wishes.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: What is a Lasting Power of Attorney (LPA), and what are the two types?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: The donor appoints an attorney to make decisions if they lose capacity. Two types: Health & Welfare and Property & Financial Affairs.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: Which LPA covers medical treatment, and what are the key conditions?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: Only the Health & Welfare LPA covers medical treatment, and only once the donor lacks capacity. It covers life-sustaining treatment only if expressly stated, and must be registered with the Office of the Public Guardian.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: What are the limits on an attorney's power under a Health & Welfare LPA?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: The attorney must act in the donor's best interests — they cannot demand treatment clinicians judge inappropriate, and cannot consent to something a valid later ADRT has already refused.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: What is an advance statement, and what is its legal weight?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: A written/verbal statement of wishes, preferences, values and beliefs (e.g. 'I'd prefer to die at home'). It is NOT legally binding, but must be taken into account in any best-interests decision.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: State the 'later document wins' interaction rule.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: Between an ADRT and an LPA for the same treatment, the later document takes precedence: an LPA made after an ADRT can override it; an ADRT made after an LPA overrides the attorney.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: What does a valid, applicable ADRT override?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: It overrides both the best-interests provision and the Court of Protection (the court can only rule on whether the ADRT is valid/applicable, not overrule a valid one).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: What is the order of authority when a patient lacks capacity?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: Valid applicable ADRT (refusals) -> Health & Welfare LPA / court-appointed deputy -> best-interests decision by the clinical team (considering advance statements, family views, and an IMCA where required).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: Can family / next-of-kin consent to or refuse treatment for an adult who lacks capacity?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: No — unless they hold a Health & Welfare LPA (or are a court-appointed deputy). Family are consulted and their account is evidence of wishes, but they cannot themselves consent or refuse.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: What is a DNACPR decision, and what does it cover?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: 'Do Not Attempt CPR' — a clinical decision recorded in the notes that CPR should not be attempted if the heart/breathing stops. It is specific to CPR only and does not affect any other treatment.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: Who must be involved in a DNACPR decision, and what did the Tracey judgment establish?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: DNACPR is a clinical decision (not the patient's to demand), but there is a legal duty to consult the patient (or those close to them if they lack capacity). The Tracey judgment (2014) established that a patient must be informed and involved unless doing so would cause them physical or psychological harm.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: What is ReSPECT, and is it legally binding?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: Recommended Summary Plan for Emergency Care and Treatment — a broader emergency care plan recording recommendations for CPR and the wider ceiling of treatment (admission, ICU, ventilation). It is a recommendation/summary, NOT itself legally binding (unlike an ADRT), and increasingly replaces standalone DNACPR forms.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: When must an Independent Mental Capacity Advocate (IMCA) be appointed?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: When a person lacks capacity, has no one else to consult (no family/friends, LPA or deputy), and a serious decision is needed (serious medical treatment or a change of accommodation).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: What is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back: Recurrent, brief episodes of vertigo triggered by head movement, caused by displaced otoconia (calcium-carbonate crystals) in the semicircular canals. It is the single commonest cause of vertigo and a major contributor to falls in the elderly.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: Explain the pathophysiology of BPPV.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back: Otoconia normally sit in the utricle; in BPPV they dislodge into a semicircular canal (most often the posterior canal, ~85-90%). Head movement makes the loose crystals move the endolymph abnormally, giving the brain a false signal of rotation -> vertigo + nystagmus. This is canalithiasis.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: What is the diagnostic triad of BPPV?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back: Positional trigger + very short duration (seconds, ~20-60s) + NO hearing loss or tinnitus. This triad separates BPPV from Meniere's (hearing loss/tinnitus) and vestibular neuronitis (constant/prolonged), and from central causes.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: List the causes/associations of BPPV.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back: Usually idiopathic; also head trauma, ageing, prolonged bed rest, and following vestibular neuronitis/labyrinthitis.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: What are the classic triggers and duration of BPPV episodes?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back: Triggered by head movements — classically rolling over in bed, lying down, looking up ('top-shelf vertigo'), bending forward. Each episode is very brief (~20-60 seconds) and settles if the head is kept still; the patient is well between episodes.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: Which single feature best distinguishes BPPV from Meniere's disease and labyrinthitis?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back: The absence of hearing loss and tinnitus. Meniere's has vertigo + hearing loss + tinnitus + aural fullness; labyrinthitis has vertigo + hearing loss (post-viral).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: What is the gold-standard diagnostic test for (posterior canal) BPPV, and how is it performed?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back: The Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre ('D for Diagnosis'): patient sits with head turned 45deg toward the side tested; rapidly lie them back with the head hanging ~20-30deg below the couch edge; hold and watch the eyes for ~30-60s.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: What constitutes a positive Dix-Hallpike test?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back: After a brief latency (a few seconds), rotatory (torsional) nystagmus toward the affected (lower) ear plus reproduction of the patient's vertigo; it is fatigable (lessens on repeat). Latency and fatigability point away from a central cause.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: Which test is used to diagnose horizontal (lateral) canal BPPV?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back: The supine roll test (not Dix-Hallpike). Horizontal-canal BPPV is less common than posterior-canal BPPV.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: Is imaging needed to diagnose BPPV?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back: No — no imaging is needed for typical BPPV. Reserve MRI for atypical features or central red flags.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: What is the first-line treatment for posterior-canal BPPV?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back: The Epley manoeuvre ('E for treatment') — a canalith repositioning procedure that rolls the otoconia out of the posterior canal back into the utricle. Highly effective (often after 1-2 attempts; Cochrane-supported).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: What are Brandt-Daroff exercises, and how do they compare to Epley?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back: Patient-performed home exercises — an option if Epley is unavailable/untolerated or for residual symptoms. They are less effective than the Epley manoeuvre.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: Why are vestibular sedatives NOT recommended in BPPV?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back: Antihistamines/vestibular sedatives (betahistine, prochlorperazine, cinnarizine) have little benefit in BPPV, don't address the mechanical cause, and may delay central compensation. (Contrast vestibular neuronitis, where short-term prochlorperazine IS used.)

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: What is the natural course of BPPV?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back: Self-limiting — most cases resolve within weeks to ~6 months even untreated, but repositioning (Epley) speeds resolution dramatically. Recurrence is common (~50% over years).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: What safety advice should you give a patient with BPPV, especially if elderly?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back: Counsel on falls risk, not driving when dizzy, and occupational hazards. BPPV is a major contributor to falls in older people.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: List the central red flags that should prompt urgent imaging/stroke pathway in a patient with vertigo.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back: Vertical or direction-changing nystagmus, other neurological signs (ataxia, diplopia, dysarthria, limb/CN signs), inability to stand/walk, severe headache, and sudden persistent vertigo — think posterior-circulation stroke.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: How does the nystagmus of BPPV differ from that of a central cause?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back: BPPV (peripheral): unilateral, horizontal-rotatory, fatigable, with latency. Central: vertical / bidirectional / direction-changing, non-fatiguing, often with other neuro signs.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: When should a patient with suspected BPPV be referred to ENT / a balance clinic?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back: If the diagnosis is uncertain, there are atypical/central features, symptoms persist despite repeated repositioning, or there is frequent recurrence. Surgery (posterior-canal occlusion) is a last resort for intractable cases.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: Give the key differentials for BPPV and their distinguishing features.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back: Meniere's — vertigo + hearing loss + tinnitus + aural fullness. Vestibular neuronitis — constant, prolonged, post-viral, NO hearing loss. Labyrinthitis — like neuronitis but WITH hearing loss. Central (stroke/tumour/MS) — neuro signs, abnormal nystagmus.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: What does the HINTS examination help distinguish?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back: It helps differentiate a peripheral cause of acute vestibular syndrome from a central (e.g. posterior-circulation stroke) cause at the bedside (Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: What is comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA)?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back: A multidimensional, multidisciplinary diagnostic and therapeutic process that assesses an older person's medical, functional, psychological, and social capabilities and problems, to build a coordinated, integrated plan for treatment and follow-up.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: What are the two defining pillars of CGA?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back: It is multidimensional (assesses several domains, not just the presenting complaint) and multidisciplinary (delivered by a team, not one doctor). Remember: holistic + team-based + iterative plan.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: Is CGA a questionnaire or a score?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back: Neither — CGA is a process. Its output is a problem list and a coordinated, patient-centred management plan that is revisited iteratively.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: Why does CGA exist / what problem does it solve?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back: Older people with frailty and multimorbidity don't fit the 'one patient, one diagnosis' model. A standard disease-focused clerking misses the falls, cognition, polypharmacy, and isolation — CGA catches all of these at once.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: What is the key outcome evidence for CGA?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back: Older people with moderate-severe frailty admitted as an emergency who receive CGA are more likely to be alive and living in their own home at follow-up, and less likely to be institutionalised (Cochrane / British Geriatrics Society). Also better function, shorter length of stay, fewer readmissions.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: Name the six domains of CGA (British Geriatrics Society framework).
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back: Physical/medical, Psychological, Functional, Social, Environmental, and Future wishes.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: What does the PHYSICAL/medical domain of CGA cover?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back: Comorbidities/multimorbidity, frailty syndromes (falls, immobility, incontinence, delirium), medication review/polypharmacy, continence, nutrition, pain, and sensory (vision/hearing) and skin. Tools: problem list, STOPP/START, bloods, MUST (nutrition).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: What does the PSYCHOLOGICAL domain cover, and which tools are used?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back: Cognition (dementia, delirium) and mood (depression, anxiety), plus mental capacity. Tools: AMTS/MoCA/MMSE for cognition, 4AT for delirium, Geriatric Depression Scale for mood.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: What does the FUNCTIONAL domain cover, and which tools are used?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back: Basic ADLs and instrumental ADLs (IADLs), mobility, balance, and gait. Tools: Barthel Index (ADLs) and the Timed Up-and-Go test.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: Distinguish basic ADLs from instrumental ADLs (IADLs).
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back: Basic ADLs = self-care: washing, dressing, feeding, toileting, transfers. IADLs = more complex independent-living tasks: cooking, shopping, managing finances, managing medications, using transport.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: What do the SOCIAL and ENVIRONMENTAL domains cover?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back: Social: care/support network, informal carers (and carer strain), formal care package, finances, safeguarding. Environmental: home setup, falls hazards, aids/adaptations, access — assessed by an occupational-therapy home assessment.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: What does the FUTURE WISHES domain of CGA cover?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back: Advance care planning, ADRT/LPA, ceilings of treatment, ReSPECT/DNACPR, and preferred place of care.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: Who are the core members of the CGA multidisciplinary team?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back: Geriatrician/medical lead, nurses, physiotherapist (mobility/balance/falls), occupational therapist (function/ADLs/home assessment), pharmacist (polypharmacy review), dietitian, SALT, and social worker — with the patient and family/carers at the centre.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: Which team member primarily assesses ADLs, home environment, and aids/adaptations?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back: The occupational therapist (OT).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: Which team member leads medication optimisation and polypharmacy review in CGA?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back: The pharmacist (using tools like STOPP/START).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: Outline the five steps of the CGA process.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back: (1) Identify the right patients (frailty screen — e.g. Clinical Frailty Scale, PRISMA-7, gait speed). (2) Multidimensional assessment across domains. (3) MDT meeting to synthesise a shared problem list. (4) Coordinated management plan with patient-centred goals. (5) Implement, review and iterate with defined follow-up.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: Which patients should CGA be targeted at?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back: Older people with frailty and multimorbidity — those who benefit most — identified with a frailty tool (Clinical Frailty Scale, PRISMA-7, gait speed). Not every older patient.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: In which settings is CGA delivered, and where is the evidence strongest?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back: Acute 'front-door' frailty units / ED / Same Day Emergency Care, inpatient geriatric wards (strongest evidence), community and home-based, perioperative (POPS — proactive care of older people undergoing surgery), and oncology (fitness for treatment).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: What are the 'geriatric giants' / frailty syndromes that CGA is designed to surface?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back: Falls, immobility, delirium/confusion, incontinence, and iatrogenic harm (polypharmacy) — the syndromes a disease-focused clerking tends to miss.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: What is deconditioning, and how does CGA address it?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back: The harm of unnecessary bed rest (loss of muscle strength and function). Urgent/front-door CGA aims to prevent unnecessary admission and deconditioning and to promote early mobilisation.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: What is delirium?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: An acute, fluctuating disturbance of consciousness, attention, cognition, and perception (an acute confusional state) that develops over hours to days and is caused by an underlying physical trigger.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: Why does delirium matter clinically?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: It is a 'geriatric giant', very common in unwell older inpatients, a marker of serious illness (roughly doubles mortality, predicts future dementia and institutionalisation), and is often reversible if the cause is found and treated — yet it is massively under-recognised (especially the hypoactive form).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: Delirium is a symptom, not a diagnosis — what does this mean for management?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: Delirium is a 'flashing light' signalling an acute physical problem. You must always find and treat the underlying cause; the management is treat the cause + supportive/environmental care, with drugs a reluctant last resort.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: What is the hallmark cognitive feature of delirium?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: Inattention (markedly impaired attention) — the defining feature, alongside acute onset and a fluctuating course.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: Contrast delirium with dementia (onset, course, consciousness, attention, reversibility).
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: Delirium: acute onset (hours-days), fluctuating course (worse at night), impaired/altered consciousness, markedly impaired attention, usually reversible. Dementia: insidious (months-years), stable/slowly progressive, normal consciousness (until late), attention relatively preserved early, irreversible.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: How do hallucinations differ between delirium and dementia?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: Hallucinations (often visual) are common in delirium; they are less common in dementia — except dementia with Lewy bodies, where visual hallucinations are characteristic.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: If you cannot tell whether a patient has delirium, dementia, or delirium-on-dementia, what should you do?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: Treat the delirium first (NICE). Obtain a collateral history to establish the cognitive baseline.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: Name the three motor subtypes of delirium.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: Hyperactive (agitated, restless, aggressive, hallucinating, wandering), Hypoactive (withdrawn, quiet, drowsy, slow), and Mixed (fluctuates between the two).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: Which motor subtype of delirium is the commonest and most dangerous, and why?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: Hypoactive delirium — it is the commonest and most dangerous because it is missed (mistaken for depression, fatigue, or 'just dementia') and carries worse outcomes. Actively look for it.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: List predisposing risk factors for delirium.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: Older age, pre-existing dementia/cognitive impairment, frailty, sensory impairment (poor vision/hearing), previous delirium, multimorbidity, and polypharmacy.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: List precipitating risk factors for delirium.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: Acute illness/infection, surgery (especially hip fracture), new drugs, dehydration, pain, catheterisation, and change of environment.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: What does the 'PINCH ME' mnemonic for delirium causes stand for?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: Pain, Infection (UTI, pneumonia, sepsis), Nutrition/poor intake, Constipation (and urinary retention), Hydration (dehydration), Medication (opioids, anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, steroids; and withdrawal) & Metabolic, Environment & Electrolytes.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: Which are the 'big two' groups of delirium causes to always consider?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: Infection (UTI, pneumonia, sepsis) and drugs/medication (including new drugs and withdrawal). Also think metabolic disturbance, constipation/retention, and intracranial causes.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: Which medications are commonly deliriogenic?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: Opioids, anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, and steroids; also withdrawal from alcohol or benzodiazepines. A medication review is a core part of assessment.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: What is the recommended UK screening tool for delirium, and its components?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: The 4AT (NICE CG103): (1) Alertness, (2) AMT-4 (age, date of birth, place, year), (3) Attention — months of the year backwards, (4) Acute change/fluctuation. A score ≥4 suggests possible delirium.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: Which delirium screening tool is used in critical care/ICU?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: CAM-ICU (rather than the 4AT).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: What investigations help find the cause of delirium?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: Observations/sepsis screen; bloods (FBC, U&E, calcium, glucose, LFTs, TFTs, CRP, magnesium); urinalysis/culture (cautiously); CXR; ECG; medication review; and CT head if focal signs, head injury, or no cause is found. Take a collateral history for baseline.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: Why must you be cautious about diagnosing a UTI as the cause of delirium in an older person?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is common in the elderly — a positive urine dip alone does not prove a UTI is the cause. Don't anchor on it; keep looking for other precipitants (per PINCH ME).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: What is the definitive treatment of delirium?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: Treat the underlying cause(s) — e.g. antibiotics for infection, analgesia for pain, rehydration, relieve constipation/retention, stop the culprit drug, correct electrolytes.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: What is the first-line management of the delirium itself (before any drugs)?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: Non-pharmacological/supportive care: reorientation (clocks, calendars, familiar objects, staff introductions), involve family/carers, optimise environment (lighting, quiet, normal sleep-wake cycle), sensory aids (glasses/hearing aids), mobilise, hydrate, attend to nutrition and bowels/bladder, avoid catheters/lines, manage pain, and verbal/non-verbal de-escalation.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: When and how should medication be used in delirium?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: Last resort only — if the patient is distressed or a risk to themselves/others AND de-escalation has failed. Use short-term, lowest-dose haloperidol (usually ≤1 week), heeding the MHRA warning on cardiac (QTc) and neurological effects. Review daily.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: In which patients must you AVOID antipsychotics (haloperidol) for delirium, and what is used instead?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies — antipsychotics cause severe extrapyramidal reactions. Use a benzodiazepine (e.g. lorazepam) instead.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: What is first-line for delirium due to alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: Benzodiazepines (e.g. chlordiazepoxide) — NOT antipsychotics.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: Do antipsychotics treat or prevent delirium?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: No — antipsychotics do not treat or prevent delirium; they only manage severe distress until the cause is corrected. Avoid physical restraint and, where possible, sedation — they worsen delirium and cause harm.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: How is delirium prevented in at-risk inpatients?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: Multicomponent prevention: orientation, early mobilisation, hydration/nutrition, sleep hygiene, sensory aids, pain control, avoiding constipation, and medication review to avoid deliriogenic drugs. Prevention is more effective than treatment.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: What is the prognosis after an episode of delirium?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: It often resolves as the cause is treated but can take weeks (and sometimes doesn't fully resolve). An episode is associated with increased mortality, longer admission, functional decline, and later dementia — so follow up and assess cognition after recovery.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: What are the Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards (DoLS)?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: The legal framework under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 for lawfully authorising the deprivation of liberty of a person who lacks capacity to consent to their care arrangements, in a hospital or care home, where those arrangements are in their best interests.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: Why does DoLS exist / which right does it protect?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: People with dementia, delirium, severe learning disability or brain injury may need to be kept somewhere and stopped from leaving for their own safety. Doing this without legal authorisation breaches their Article 5 (right to liberty). DoLS makes protective confinement lawful and scrutinised rather than arbitrary.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: To whom and in which settings does DoLS apply?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: Adults ≥18 who lack capacity to consent to their care/treatment arrangements, in a hospital or care home.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: What is the classic 'acid test' (Cheshire West 2014) for a deprivation of liberty?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: A person is deprived of liberty if ALL THREE apply: (1) they lack capacity to consent to the arrangements, (2) they are under continuous supervision and control, and (3) they are not free to leave.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: Under the acid test, did it matter whether the person was content or the arrangements benevolent?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: No. Under the acid test it did not matter whether the person was content, whether the arrangements were benevolent/in their best interests, or the purpose — if the three limbs were met, authorisation was needed.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: What did the June 2026 Supreme Court ruling (Attorney General for Northern Ireland's Reference [2026] UKSC 16) decide?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: It overruled Cheshire West and removed the bright-line acid test as the sole determinant, with immediate, UK-wide effect and no transition period. In its place is a multifactorial assessment, and it revived that a person lacking Mental Capacity Act capacity may still give valid consent to their arrangements.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: What factors are weighed in the multifactorial test of a deprivation of liberty?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: The acid-test factors remain relevant but are no longer sufficient; you weigh: the type, duration, effects and manner of the restrictions; the normality of the setting (a near-normal home/family environment weighs against a deprivation); the purpose of the measures; and whether the person objects or is content. No single factor is determinative.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: Can a person who lacks Mental Capacity Act capacity ever avoid being deprived of liberty by consenting?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: Yes — a person lacking MCA capacity who can express genuine acceptance may be giving valid consent, meaning there is no deprivation of liberty (e.g. a genuinely content person in a near-normal setting).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: What is the difference between a restriction and a deprivation of liberty?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: A difference of degree and intensity, not kind. The more continuous, controlling and total the arrangements, the more likely they cross into a deprivation requiring authorisation.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: What are the Liberty Protection Safeguards (LPS), and what is their status?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: A scheme legislated in the Mental Capacity (Amendment) Act 2019 to replace DoLS with a streamlined, all-settings, age-16+ system. It has been repeatedly delayed and is still not implemented (a government consultation was announced for 2026).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: What is the current operational position for authorising a deprivation of liberty (2026)?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: DoLS remains the operational process for hospitals and care homes (Court of Protection for other settings); it has not been abolished, and LPS is not yet implemented. When in doubt, continue using DoLS/Court of Protection processes.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: Who applies for a DoLS authorisation, and to whom?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: The Managing Authority (the hospital or care home) applies to the Supervisory Body (the local authority).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: What is an urgent DoLS authorisation?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: The managing authority can self-grant an urgent authorisation for up to 7 days while a standard authorisation is sought.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: What is a standard DoLS authorisation and how long can it last?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: The supervisory body commissions the assessments and, if met, grants a standard authorisation that is time-limited (up to 12 months) and must be reviewed.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: Name the six assessments for a standard DoLS authorisation.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: Age, mental capacity, mental health, best interests, eligibility (Mental Health Act interface), and no-refusals (checking no valid ADRT/LPA/deputy decision conflicts).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: What safeguards and challenge rights does a person under DoLS have?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: They must have a Relevant Person's Representative and access to an Independent Mental Capacity Advocate (IMCA), and a right to challenge the authorisation in the Court of Protection under section 21A.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: How must any deprivation of liberty relate to the person's interests and freedom?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: It must always be the least restrictive option and in the person's best interests.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: How is a deprivation of liberty authorised in settings other than a hospital or care home (e.g. own home, supported living)?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: By the Court of Protection (a 'COPDOL11' application), not DoLS.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: How is a deprivation of liberty handled for people under 18 (including 16-17s)?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: Via the Court of Protection / inherent jurisdiction (not DoLS, which applies only to adults ≥18).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: When might the Mental Health Act be the correct route instead of DoLS?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: If the person is detainable under the Mental Health Act for treatment of a mental disorder and objects, the MHA may be the correct route — the MHA/MCA interface is a recognised complexity.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: How does DoLS fit within the wider Mental Capacity Act framework?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: DoLS/LPS sit within the MCA — all five principles apply (presume capacity, support decision-making, unwise decisions aren't incapacity, best interests, least restrictive). It presupposes a 2-stage capacity assessment and a best-interests determination.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.question: Which of the following is one of the five statutory principles of the Mental Capacity Act 2005?
options: Capacity must be proven before any treatment
A person is not to be treated as unable to decide merely because the decision is unwise
Relatives automatically decide for an incapacitated adult
The most protective option should always be chosen
Capacity, once lost, is presumed permanent
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.answer: A person is not to be treated as unable to decide merely because the decision is unwise
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.explanation: An UNWISE decision does not equal a lack of capacity — a core MCA principle. Others: capacity is PRESUMED (not proven first); relatives do not automatically decide; the LEAST restrictive option is chosen; capacity is decision- and time-specific, not permanently lost.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.question: A 78-year-old man with mild dementia refuses an operation clinicians recommend. He can explain the operation, its risks and alternatives, remembers the discussion, weighs it up, and communicates a clear 'no'. What is the correct interpretation?
options: He lacks capacity because he has dementia
He lacks capacity because the decision is unwise
He has capacity for this decision and his refusal must be respected
A best-interests decision should override him
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.answer: He has capacity for this decision and his refusal must be respected
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.explanation: Capacity is decision-specific and functional: he can understand, retain, weigh and communicate, so he HAS capacity for this decision regardless of a dementia diagnosis or the wisdom of his choice. A capacitous refusal must be respected; best interests and family do not apply while he has capacity.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.question: What are the four abilities assessed in stage 2 (the functional test) of the Mental Capacity Act capacity assessment?
options: Understand, retain, use/weigh, and communicate the decision
Orientation to time, place, person, and situation
Recall of past medical, drug, and social history
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.answer: Understand, retain, use/weigh, and communicate the decision
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.explanation: The MCA functional test asks whether the person can UNDERSTAND the relevant information, RETAIN it, USE OR WEIGH it, and COMMUNICATE their decision. Failure of any one (due to an impairment of mind/brain) means they lack capacity for that decision.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.question: For an Advance Decision to Refuse Treatment (ADRT) to validly refuse life-sustaining treatment, which additional requirement must be met?
options: It must be reviewed annually by a GP
It must be written, signed and witnessed, and state it applies 'even if life is at risk'
It must be approved by the Court of Protection
It must be countersigned by two consultants
It must be registered with the Office of the Public Guardian
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.answer: It must be written, signed and witnessed, and state it applies 'even if life is at risk'
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.explanation: To refuse LIFE-SUSTAINING treatment, an ADRT must be in writing, signed and witnessed, and explicitly state it applies 'even if life is at risk'. Annual review, court approval, consultant countersignature and OPG registration (which applies to LPAs) are not requirements.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.question: Which single statement about an Advance Decision to Refuse Treatment is correct?
options: It can be used to request a specific treatment
A valid, applicable ADRT is legally binding and has the same force as a competent patient's refusal
It can refuse basic care such as warmth and oral food/fluids
It is only advisory and can be overridden in the patient's best interests
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.answer: A valid, applicable ADRT is legally binding and has the same force as a competent patient's refusal
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.explanation: A valid and applicable ADRT is LEGALLY BINDING — the same force as a contemporaneous refusal by a capacitous patient. It can only REFUSE (never demand) treatment, cannot authorise euthanasia (illegal in the UK), and cannot refuse basic care/symptom relief.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.question: Which type of Lasting Power of Attorney allows an attorney to make decisions about medical treatment?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.explanation: Only the HEALTH AND WELFARE LPA covers medical treatment, and only once the donor lacks capacity; it covers life-sustaining treatment only if expressly stated. The Property and Financial Affairs LPA covers money/property, not treatment.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.question: A registered Health and Welfare LPA must be registered with which body before it can be used?
options: The Office of the Public Guardian
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.answer: The Office of the Public Guardian
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.explanation: An LPA must be registered with the OFFICE OF THE PUBLIC GUARDIAN to be valid. The Court of Protection resolves disputes and can appoint deputies but does not register LPAs; the CQC, GMC and safeguarding boards have other roles.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.question: What is the legal status of an advance statement of wishes and preferences?
options: Not legally binding, but must be taken into account in best-interests decisions
Binding only if it refuses treatment
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.answer: Not legally binding, but must be taken into account in best-interests decisions
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.explanation: An advance statement (wishes, values, preferences) is NOT legally binding but MUST be considered when a best-interests decision is made after capacity is lost. It differs from an ADRT (binding refusal) and remains highly relevant, not irrelevant.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.question: A patient made a valid ADRT refusing a treatment, and later (while still capacitous) made a Health and Welfare LPA covering the same treatment. Which document takes precedence?
options: The ADRT, because refusals always win
The later LPA, because the later document takes precedence
Neither is valid once two documents exist
The Court of Protection must decide
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.answer: The later LPA, because the later document takes precedence
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.explanation: Under the 'later document wins' rule, an LPA made AFTER an ADRT (covering the same treatment) can override it. Conversely, an ADRT made after an LPA overrides the attorney. Here the LPA is later, so it takes precedence.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.question: An 82-year-old woman is unconscious after a large stroke. She has a valid, applicable written ADRT (signed, witnessed, stating 'even if life is at risk') refusing mechanical ventilation. Her son insists she would 'want everything done'. What should the team do?
options: Ventilate her, because the family's wishes take priority
Follow the ADRT and not ventilate, as it is legally binding
Apply to the Court of Protection to override the ADRT
Make a best-interests decision ignoring the ADRT
Ventilate her until the LPA can be located
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.answer: Follow the ADRT and not ventilate, as it is legally binding
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.explanation: A valid, applicable ADRT refusing ventilation is legally binding and must be followed — it overrides both best-interests decision-making and the Court of Protection. Family cannot consent or refuse for her (they hold no LPA); their account is evidence, not authority.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.question: An unconscious man lacks capacity, has NO ADRT, NO LPA and NO court-appointed deputy, and needs a decision about serious treatment. His family are contactable. What is the correct process?
options: The family formally consent on his behalf
A best-interests decision is made by the clinical team, consulting the family and any advance statement
Treatment is withheld until he regains capacity
An IMCA must be appointed before any decision
The most senior doctor decides alone without consultation
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.answer: A best-interests decision is made by the clinical team, consulting the family and any advance statement
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.explanation: With no ADRT/LPA/deputy, the clinical team makes a BEST-INTERESTS decision, consulting those close to him (who inform but cannot consent) and any advance statement. An IMCA is required only when there is NO ONE to consult; here the family are available, so an IMCA is not mandated.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.question: Regarding a DNACPR decision, which statement is correct?
options: It means the patient will receive no active treatment at all
It applies only to cardiopulmonary resuscitation and not to other treatments
It requires the patient's consent to be valid
It must be authorised by the Court of Protection
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.answer: It applies only to cardiopulmonary resuscitation and not to other treatments
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.explanation: A DNACPR decision relates ONLY to CPR — all other appropriate treatment (antibiotics, fluids, ICU where indicated) continues. It is a clinical decision that does not require patient consent, but the patient (or those close to them) must be consulted/informed (Tracey judgment).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.question: A DNACPR order is placed for a competent patient who is never told or consulted, without any reason that discussion would cause harm. Which principle has been breached?
options: The Tracey judgment requirement to inform and involve the patient
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.answer: The Tracey judgment requirement to inform and involve the patient
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.explanation: The Tracey judgment (2014) established that a patient must be informed of and involved in a DNACPR decision unless doing so would cause them physical or psychological harm. Failing to consult a competent patient without such justification breaches this duty. Bolam/Bolitho concern negligence standards; Gillick concerns children's competence.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.question: How does ReSPECT differ from an ADRT?
options: ReSPECT is legally binding whereas an ADRT is only advisory
ReSPECT is a recommendation/summary of emergency care that is not itself legally binding, whereas a valid ADRT is legally binding
They are identical documents with different names
ReSPECT can only be completed by the patient, not clinicians
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.answer: ReSPECT is a recommendation/summary of emergency care that is not itself legally binding, whereas a valid ADRT is legally binding
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.explanation: ReSPECT records recommendations for CPR and the wider ceiling of emergency treatment; it is a summary/recommendation and is NOT itself legally binding. A valid, applicable ADRT, by contrast, IS legally binding. ReSPECT is completed collaboratively (clinician + patient/those close).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.question: A capacitous 40-year-old Jehovah's Witness refuses a life-saving blood transfusion after major haemorrhage, fully understanding she may die. What is the correct action?
options: Transfuse her in her best interests
Respect her refusal, as a capacitous adult may refuse any treatment even if life-saving
Declare her to lack capacity because the decision is unwise
Apply to court to authorise transfusion
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.answer: Respect her refusal, as a capacitous adult may refuse any treatment even if life-saving
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.explanation: A capacitous adult may refuse ANY treatment, including life-saving treatment, for any or no reason; an unwise decision is not incapacity. Her informed refusal must be respected — best interests, family consent and court applications do not apply while she has capacity.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.question: An attorney under a registered Health and Welfare LPA demands a treatment that the clinical team judges to be futile and not in the patient's interest. What is the correct position?
options: The attorney's demand must be followed
The attorney cannot demand treatment clinicians judge inappropriate; they must act in the donor's best interests
The attorney's power is invalid once the patient lacks capacity
The family can overrule the attorney
The treatment must be given pending a court ruling
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.answer: The attorney cannot demand treatment clinicians judge inappropriate; they must act in the donor's best interests
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.explanation: An attorney must act in the donor's BEST INTERESTS and cannot demand treatment that clinicians judge inappropriate/futile, nor consent to something a valid later ADRT refuses. The LPA becomes usable precisely WHEN the donor lacks capacity, so the power is not invalid then.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.question: In benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, what is the underlying mechanism?
options: Displaced otoconia moving freely within a semicircular canal (canalithiasis)
Post-viral inflammation of the vestibular nerve
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.answer: Displaced otoconia moving freely within a semicircular canal (canalithiasis)
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.explanation: BPPV is caused by CANALITHIASIS — otoconia (calcium-carbonate crystals) displaced from the utricle into a semicircular canal, moving the endolymph abnormally and signalling false rotation. Endolymphatic hydrops is Meniere's; post-viral nerve inflammation is vestibular neuronitis; demyelination/ischaemia are central causes.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.question: Which semicircular canal is most commonly involved in BPPV?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.explanation: The POSTERIOR canal is involved in about 85-90% of BPPV (its position makes it most likely to collect displaced otoconia). Horizontal-canal BPPV is less common and is diagnosed with the supine roll test; anterior-canal BPPV is rare.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.question: A 72-year-old woman describes brief spinning sensations lasting under a minute whenever she rolls over in bed or looks up to a high shelf. She has no hearing loss or tinnitus and is well between episodes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.explanation: The triad of a positional trigger, very brief episodes (seconds), and NO hearing loss/tinnitus is classic BPPV. Meniere's has hearing loss/tinnitus/fullness; vestibular neuronitis is constant and prolonged; stroke gives persistent vertigo with neuro signs; vestibular migraine has headache/migraine features.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.question: Which test is the gold-standard for diagnosing posterior-canal BPPV?
options: The head impulse test in isolation
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.explanation: The DIX-HALLPIKE manoeuvre is diagnostic for posterior-canal BPPV ('D for Diagnosis'). The supine roll test is for horizontal-canal BPPV; the Epley manoeuvre is the TREATMENT; the head impulse test is one component of HINTS; audiometry assesses hearing (normal in BPPV).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.question: During a Dix-Hallpike test, which finding indicates a positive result consistent with BPPV rather than a central cause?
options: Immediate, sustained, vertical nystagmus with no latency
Torsional nystagmus toward the lower ear after a brief latency, which is fatigable
Direction-changing nystagmus that does not fatigue
Nystagmus only when the eyes are closed
No nystagmus but severe persistent headache
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.answer: Torsional nystagmus toward the lower ear after a brief latency, which is fatigable
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.explanation: A positive Dix-Hallpike shows, after a brief LATENCY, torsional (rotatory) nystagmus toward the affected (lower) ear with reproduced vertigo, and it is FATIGABLE. Immediate, non-fatiguing, vertical or direction-changing nystagmus suggests a CENTRAL cause and warrants imaging.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.question: A patient has a positive Dix-Hallpike test confirming right posterior-canal BPPV. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.explanation: First-line treatment for confirmed posterior-canal BPPV is the EPLEY manoeuvre, which repositions the otoconia back into the utricle and is often curative. Vestibular sedatives are not recommended; betahistine/low-salt is for Meniere's; MRI and surgery are reserved for atypical/central or intractable cases.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.question: A 68-year-old man is prescribed regular prochlorperazine for several weeks for typical BPPV, with little improvement. What is the problem with this management?
options: Vestibular sedatives are not recommended in BPPV and may delay central compensation; repositioning is the treatment
He should also be started on betahistine
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.answer: Vestibular sedatives are not recommended in BPPV and may delay central compensation; repositioning is the treatment
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.explanation: Vestibular sedatives/antihistamines have little benefit in BPPV, do not address the mechanical cause, and may DELAY central compensation. The effective treatment is a canalith repositioning (Epley) manoeuvre. (Short-term prochlorperazine is appropriate in vestibular neuronitis, not BPPV.)

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.question: A 70-year-old presents with sudden, persistent vertigo that does not stop when still, vertical nystagmus, and difficulty walking unaided. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Perform the Epley manoeuvre and discharge
Assess for a central cause (e.g. posterior-circulation stroke) and arrange urgent imaging
Prescribe cinnarizine and review in 6 weeks
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.answer: Assess for a central cause (e.g. posterior-circulation stroke) and arrange urgent imaging
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.explanation: Persistent (non-positional) vertigo, VERTICAL nystagmus, and inability to walk are central red flags pointing to a posterior-circulation stroke. This requires urgent assessment (HINTS) and imaging, not bedside repositioning or vestibular sedatives.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.question: A 55-year-old woman has recurrent vertigo lasting hours, with a roaring tinnitus, fluctuating hearing loss, and a sensation of fullness in one ear. Which diagnosis does this fit, distinguishing it from BPPV?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.explanation: Vertigo lasting hours WITH hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness is MENIERE'S disease (endolymphatic hydrops) — the presence of cochlear symptoms and longer duration separate it from BPPV, which is brief, positional, and has no hearing loss/tinnitus.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.question: What is the approximate duration of a single BPPV vertigo episode?
options: A few seconds up to about a minute
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.answer: A few seconds up to about a minute
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.explanation: BPPV episodes are very brief — typically about 20-60 seconds — and settle when the head is kept still. Episodes lasting hours suggest Meniere's; constant vertigo for days suggests vestibular neuronitis or a central cause.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.question: Which is the single commonest cause of vertigo?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.explanation: BPPV is the single commonest cause of vertigo. It is also an important, treatable contributor to falls in older adults.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.question: A patient successfully treated with the Epley manoeuvre asks about the future. What is the most accurate counselling regarding recurrence?
options: BPPV essentially never recurs once treated
Recurrence is common (around 50% over several years) and repositioning can be repeated
Recurrence means the Epley was done incorrectly
Lifelong vestibular sedatives are needed to prevent recurrence
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.answer: Recurrence is common (around 50% over several years) and repositioning can be repeated
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.explanation: BPPV recurs in roughly half of patients over the following years; the Epley manoeuvre can simply be repeated. Recurrence does not imply sinister pathology or incorrect technique, and long-term vestibular sedatives are not indicated.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.question: A patient has vertigo provoked by rolling side to side while lying flat, and the Dix-Hallpike is unremarkable. Which test should be performed to look for a less common form of BPPV?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.explanation: Horizontal (lateral) canal BPPV is diagnosed with the SUPINE ROLL test, not the Dix-Hallpike. It is less common than posterior-canal BPPV but should be considered when the history is positional but Dix-Hallpike is negative.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.question: Which statement about imaging in typical BPPV is correct?
options: CT head is mandatory before treatment
No imaging is required for typical BPPV; MRI is reserved for atypical or central features
MRI is required in every case to confirm canalithiasis
Carotid Doppler is the first-line investigation
An X-ray of the skull confirms the diagnosis
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.answer: No imaging is required for typical BPPV; MRI is reserved for atypical or central features
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.explanation: Typical BPPV is a clinical/bedside diagnosis (positive Dix-Hallpike) and needs NO imaging. MRI is reserved for atypical presentations or central red flags. Canalithiasis is not visible on routine imaging.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.question: Following which condition can BPPV develop as a recognised association?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.explanation: BPPV is often idiopathic but is recognised after head trauma, with ageing, after prolonged bed rest, and FOLLOWING vestibular neuronitis/labyrinthitis. The other conditions are not the classic antecedents of BPPV.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.question: Which statement best describes comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA)?
options: A multidimensional, multidisciplinary process producing a coordinated care plan
A screening blood-test panel for older adults
A one-off assessment performed by the admitting doctor alone
A questionnaire completed by the patient at home
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.answer: A multidimensional, multidisciplinary process producing a coordinated care plan
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.explanation: CGA is a multidimensional (several domains) and multidisciplinary (team-delivered) PROCESS that yields a coordinated, patient-centred management plan reviewed iteratively. It is not a score, a blood panel, a single-clinician clerking, or a self-completed questionnaire.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.question: Which of the following is one of the domains assessed in CGA?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.explanation: CGA domains are physical/medical, psychological, FUNCTIONAL (ADLs/IADLs, mobility), social, environmental, and future wishes. The other options are not CGA domains.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.question: An 86-year-old woman is admitted after recurrent falls. She has dementia, takes 11 medications, is incontinent, and her daughter (main carer) is exhausted. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Comprehensive geriatric assessment with the multidisciplinary team
Discharge once the acute issue is treated, with no further review
Referral to a single specialist for the falls alone
Commence long-term bed rest for safety
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.answer: Comprehensive geriatric assessment with the multidisciplinary team
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.explanation: This frail, multimorbid patient with falls, cognitive impairment, polypharmacy, incontinence and carer strain is the ideal candidate for CGA — a multidimensional, MDT process addressing all these problems together. A single-organ work-up or isolated referral would miss the interacting issues; bed rest causes deconditioning.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.question: The strongest evidence for CGA improving outcomes (being alive and in one's own home, with less institutionalisation) comes from which setting?
options: Routine outpatient clinics for fit older adults
Emergency admission of frail older people to inpatient geriatric wards
Screening of the entire population over 65
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.answer: Emergency admission of frail older people to inpatient geriatric wards
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.explanation: Cochrane/BGS evidence is strongest for CGA in frail older people admitted as an EMERGENCY to inpatient geriatric care: they are more likely to be alive and in their own home and less likely to be institutionalised. CGA is targeted at the frail, not the whole older population.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.question: Which tool is most appropriate for assessing the FUNCTIONAL domain (basic activities of daily living) in CGA?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.explanation: The Barthel Index assesses basic ADLs (function). The 4AT screens for delirium (psychological), the Geriatric Depression Scale for mood, STOPP/START for medication appropriateness, and MUST for nutrition.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.question: Which tool is used within CGA specifically to screen for delirium?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.explanation: The 4AT is a rapid delirium screening tool (part of the psychological/cognitive domain). Barthel and Timed Up-and-Go assess function/mobility, MUST assesses nutrition, and PRISMA-7 is a frailty-identification tool.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.question: Which activity is an instrumental activity of daily living (IADL) rather than a basic ADL?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.explanation: IADLs are more complex independent-living tasks such as managing finances/medications, shopping, cooking and using transport. Dressing, feeding, transfers and toileting are basic ADLs (self-care).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.question: Which member of the CGA multidisciplinary team is best placed to assess the home environment, falls hazards, and aids/adaptations?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.explanation: The occupational therapist assesses function/ADLs and performs the home/environmental assessment, recommending aids and adaptations. The pharmacist reviews medication, the dietitian nutrition, and SALT swallow/communication.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.question: What is the correct FIRST step of the CGA process?
options: Identify the right patients using a frailty screen
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.answer: Identify the right patients using a frailty screen
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.explanation: CGA begins by IDENTIFYING the patients who will benefit — older people with frailty/multimorbidity, screened with a tool such as the Clinical Frailty Scale, PRISMA-7 or gait speed. Assessment, MDT synthesis, planning, and review/follow-up come afterwards.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.question: A previously independent, non-frail 68-year-old is admitted with a single, straightforward problem (an ankle fracture) and no other issues. Is full comprehensive geriatric assessment specifically indicated?
options: Yes, every patient over 65 requires CGA
No, CGA is targeted at frail, multimorbid older people rather than every older patient
Yes, because he is over the retirement age
No, because CGA is only for people over 90
Yes, CGA is mandatory before any fracture treatment
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.answer: No, CGA is targeted at frail, multimorbid older people rather than every older patient
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.explanation: CGA is TARGETED at those who benefit most — frail, multimorbid older people — not every older patient. A fit, independent person with a single problem does not specifically require the full CGA process (though good care still applies).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.question: Which cluster represents the 'geriatric giants' / frailty syndromes that CGA is designed to surface?
options: Falls, immobility, delirium, incontinence, and iatrogenic harm (polypharmacy)
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.answer: Falls, immobility, delirium, incontinence, and iatrogenic harm (polypharmacy)
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.explanation: The geriatric giants/frailty syndromes are falls, immobility, delirium/confusion, incontinence, and iatrogenic harm (polypharmacy). CGA is structured precisely to detect and manage these often-missed, interacting problems.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.question: What does 'POPS' refer to as a setting for CGA?
options: Proactive care of Older People undergoing Surgery (perioperative CGA)
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.answer: Proactive care of Older People undergoing Surgery (perioperative CGA)
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.explanation: POPS = Proactive care of Older People undergoing Surgery — a perioperative CGA service that optimises frail older surgical patients. CGA is also delivered in acute frailty units, wards, community/home, and oncology.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.question: Why is urgent 'front-door' CGA in the emergency department or same-day emergency care valued?
options: It guarantees admission for every frail patient
It helps avoid unnecessary admission and the deconditioning caused by bed rest
It replaces the need for any medication review
It is a legal requirement for all attendances
It is used only to speed up bed allocation
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.answer: It helps avoid unnecessary admission and the deconditioning caused by bed rest
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.explanation: Rapid CGA at the front door can prevent unnecessary admissions and the DECONDITIONING that results from bed rest, supporting safe discharge or admission-avoidance. It does not guarantee admission and is not merely an administrative step.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.question: Within CGA, which criteria set is used to guide medication review and reduce inappropriate polypharmacy?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.explanation: STOPP/START criteria guide the pharmacist-led medication review in CGA (STOPP = potentially inappropriate medications to stop; START = beneficial medications being omitted). The others are stroke/bleeding/VTE/pneumonia risk scores unrelated to polypharmacy review.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.question: What is the intended OUTPUT of the CGA process?
options: A shared problem list and a coordinated, patient-centred plan that is reviewed iteratively
A referral letter to one specialist
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.answer: A shared problem list and a coordinated, patient-centred plan that is reviewed iteratively
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.explanation: The output of CGA is a synthesised PROBLEM LIST and a coordinated, patient-centred management plan with clear (often functional) goals, implemented and then reviewed/iterated with defined follow-up — not a single diagnosis, score, or isolated referral.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.question: Which single feature is the hallmark of delirium?
options: Markedly impaired attention with an acute, fluctuating course
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.answer: Markedly impaired attention with an acute, fluctuating course
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.explanation: The hallmark of delirium is INATTENTION, with an ACUTE onset and a FLUCTUATING course. Progressive memory loss over months and stable/preserved consciousness point to dementia; delirium is characteristically acute and fluctuating, not fixed.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.question: An 82-year-old man 2 days after hip-fracture surgery becomes acutely confused and inattentive, worse at night, with visual hallucinations; his daughter says he was cognitively normal last week. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.explanation: Acute onset over days, fluctuation (worse at night), inattention and visual hallucinations after surgery in an older person are classic for DELIRIUM (here precipitated by surgery/hip fracture). The acute course and altered attention exclude a chronic dementia, and a documented normal baseline argues against a primary psychiatric diagnosis.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.question: Which motor subtype of delirium is the commonest and most frequently missed?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.explanation: HYPOACTIVE delirium (quiet, withdrawn, drowsy) is the commonest and most dangerous subtype because it is easily missed or mistaken for depression, fatigue or 'just dementia', and it carries worse outcomes. Hyperactive delirium is the more obvious form.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.question: A quiet, drowsy, withdrawn 88-year-old inpatient is assumed to be 'depressed and no trouble'. What is the most important consideration?
options: Consider hypoactive delirium and screen for an underlying acute cause
Prescribe a hypnotic to help him settle
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.answer: Consider hypoactive delirium and screen for an underlying acute cause
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.explanation: A newly quiet, drowsy, inattentive older inpatient may have HYPOACTIVE delirium, which is commonly mislabelled as depression or dementia. The priority is to recognise it and screen for a precipitant (PINCH ME) — not to start an antidepressant or hypnotic or take no action.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.question: Which is the recommended UK bedside screening tool for delirium (per NICE)?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.explanation: The 4AT is the NICE-recommended delirium screening tool (Alertness, AMT-4, Attention via months backwards, and Acute change/fluctuation); a score >=4 suggests possible delirium. The MMSE tests cognition broadly, the Barthel assesses function, and PHQ-9 screens for depression.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.question: A 4AT is performed and the score is 5. How is this interpreted?
options: Possible delirium — the diagnosis should be confirmed and the cause sought
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.answer: Possible delirium — the diagnosis should be confirmed and the cause sought
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.explanation: A 4AT score of >=4 indicates POSSIBLE delirium, prompting clinical confirmation and a search for the underlying cause. It does not exclude delirium or diagnose dementia, and a positive screen mandates action, not none.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.question: Which mnemonic best captures the common causes to screen for in delirium?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.explanation: PINCH ME screens delirium precipitants: Pain, Infection, Nutrition, Constipation, Hydration, Medication/Metabolic, Environment/Electrolytes. SOCRATES characterises pain, FAST is for stroke recognition, ABCDE is resuscitation, and CHA2DS2-VASc estimates stroke risk in AF.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.question: An agitated, distressed patient with delirium remains at risk of harm despite reorientation, family presence and verbal de-escalation. What is the most appropriate next step (in a patient without Parkinson's or Lewy body dementia)?
options: Short-term, low-dose haloperidol with daily review
Routine sedation every night for the admission
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.answer: Short-term, low-dose haloperidol with daily review
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.explanation: When non-pharmacological measures fail and the patient is distressed/at risk, a SHORT course of LOW-DOSE haloperidol is appropriate (heeding the MHRA warning), reviewed daily. Physical restraint, high-dose/long-acting sedation and routine nightly sedation worsen delirium and cause harm.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.question: A 79-year-old with Parkinson's disease develops an agitated delirium needing pharmacological calming after de-escalation fails. Which drug is most appropriate?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.explanation: Antipsychotics (haloperidol, olanzapine, risperidone, prochlorperazine) must be AVOIDED in Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies because they cause severe extrapyramidal reactions. A benzodiazepine such as LORAZEPAM is used instead when medication is unavoidable.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.question: A 60-year-old man admitted 2 days ago becomes tremulous, sweaty, tachycardic, and acutely confused with visual hallucinations; he drinks heavily and has had no alcohol since admission. What is the most appropriate pharmacological treatment?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.explanation: This is delirium from ALCOHOL WITHDRAWAL (delirium tremens), for which BENZODIAZEPINES (e.g. chlordiazepoxide) are first-line — they treat the withdrawal itself. Antipsychotics are not first-line here (they lower the seizure threshold and don't treat withdrawal).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.question: Do antipsychotics prevent or cure delirium?
options: Yes, they cure the underlying cause
No, they do not treat or prevent delirium; they only manage severe distress until the cause is corrected
Yes, they prevent delirium if given prophylactically to all inpatients
Yes, they reverse the confusion within minutes
Yes, they shorten the illness in every patient
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.answer: No, they do not treat or prevent delirium; they only manage severe distress until the cause is corrected
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.explanation: Antipsychotics do NOT treat or prevent delirium — they only manage severe distress temporarily while the underlying cause is corrected. Definitive treatment is addressing the precipitant; prophylactic antipsychotics for all inpatients are not recommended.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.question: An 84-year-old woman with acute confusion has a positive urine dipstick but no urinary symptoms, fever or raised inflammatory markers. How should this be interpreted?
options: It confirms a UTI is the cause; treat with antibiotics and stop looking
Asymptomatic bacteriuria is common in older people; do not anchor on it and continue to search for the true cause
It proves urosepsis and mandates ICU admission
It excludes any infective cause of the delirium
It indicates the delirium is factitious
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.answer: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is common in older people; do not anchor on it and continue to search for the true cause
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.explanation: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is very common in older adults, so a positive dipstick alone does not prove a UTI is the cause of delirium. Anchoring on it risks missing the real precipitant — continue the PINCH ME work-up rather than treating a presumed UTI reflexively.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.question: Which is the FIRST-LINE management of the delirium itself, alongside treating the cause?
options: Non-pharmacological measures (reorientation, sensory aids, sleep, family, mobilisation)
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.answer: Non-pharmacological measures (reorientation, sensory aids, sleep, family, mobilisation)
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.explanation: First-line management of delirium is treating the underlying cause PLUS non-pharmacological/environmental care: reorientation, glasses/hearing aids, normalising sleep, involving family, mobilising and hydrating. Drugs and restraint are last resorts, not routine measures.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.question: What is the correct action if you cannot distinguish delirium from dementia (or suspect delirium superimposed on dementia)?
options: Assume dementia and take no acute action
Treat for delirium first while establishing the baseline with a collateral history
Discharge the patient for outpatient assessment
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.answer: Treat for delirium first while establishing the baseline with a collateral history
